prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

ISLAMABAD, Pakistan (CNN) -- Pakistan's military continued its assault Thursday on militants in Taliban-held areas, its chief spokesman told reporters. Pakistani army trucks move military equipment into the troubled Buner district Thursday. So far, 14 militants have been killed in the past 24 hours, Maj. Gen. Athar Abbas said. The operation is still ongoing in the districts of Dir and Buner, which was recently seized by the Taliban in violation of an agreement with Pakistan's government. Pakistani forces have completely secured Daggar, the main town in Buner and the scene of heavy fighting on Wednesday, Abbas said. The Daggar operation resulted in the deaths of 50 militants, but freed 18 Frontier Corps personnel who had been abducted by militants, he said. Fifty-two of their colleagues are still believed to be held by their suspected Taliban kidnappers. This week's military operation has resulted in more than 180 militant casualties since Sunday, while the military has suffered one death and one injury, according to Abbas. He said he hopes the operation will be completed by the end of the week. Pakistan has asked the United States to supply its forces with helicopters, communication equipment and night vision technology, Abbas said Thursday. Most of this week's casualties happened on Tuesday, when Pakistani fighter jets launched airstrikes, killing at least 70 militants in the Dir district, according to the Pakistani military. The operation is part of the Pakistani army's intensified drive against the Taliban in its restive tribal regions. The Pakistani government has been criticized for not cracking down on militants along its border with Afghanistan. As a result, the U.S. military has carried out airstrikes against militant targets in Pakistan, which have rankled relations between the two countries. The military campaign has apparently not stopped Washington from carrying out unmanned drone attacks on Pakistan's soil. A suspected unmanned aerial vehicle killed six people Wednesday night in the village of Kaniguran in the tribal district of South Waziristan near the border with Afghanistan, Pakistani intelligence sources said. Pakistan has complained repeatedly about what it says are American airstrikes on its territory. The U.S. military in Afghanistan has not commented on the strikes, which typically target Taliban fighters in the border region. But the United States is the only country operating in the region known to have the capability to launch missiles from remote-controlled drones. U.S. President Barack Obama is "gravely concerned about the situation in Pakistan," he told reporters Wednesday night. Speaking at a news conference capping his 100th day in office, Obama said the United States has "huge national security interests in making sure that Pakistan is stable" and doesn't end up a "nuclear-armed militant state." But he stressed he was more concerned about the ability of Pakistan's civilian government to "deliver basic services," and not "that they're immediately going to be overrun" by the Taliban. Pakistan's recent military crackdown has led to an exodus of civilians from the region. At least 33,000 residents have left their homes in the midst of the recent fighting, according to Amnesty International. Civilians fleeing from Lower Dir in Pakistan's North West Frontier Province join more than 500,000 people already displaced by the fighting, the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees said. The Pakistani military completed its operation to eliminate and expel militants in Dir Tuesday, and is now focusing on the Buner district, Abbas said. About 300 militants entered Buner a few days ago, in violation of the Taliban's recent agreement to leave the district, he said. Buner is about 60 miles from Islamabad, but Abbas said the militants pose no threat of entering the capital. The fighter jets pounded targets in Buner and the Swat Valley in an effort to block the militants' entry and exit points, according to Abbas. CNN's Samson Desta, Ivan Watson, and Nasir Habib contributed to this report.

**ISLAMABAD, Pakistan (CNN) —** Pakistan’s armed forces pressed ahead Thursday with attacks against militants in Taliban-controlled territory, the military’s top spokesperson said.

Army trucks were seen transporting military hardware into the conflict-hit district of Buner. Maj. Gen. Athar Abbas told journalists that 14 militants had died during the previous 24 hours.

Military action continued in Dir and Buner, the latter having recently been taken by the Taliban despite an agreement with the Pakistani government. Abbas said government troops had gained full control of Daggar, Buner’s principal town, after intense clashes there Wednesday.

According to Abbas, 50 militants were killed during the operation in Daggar. Troops also rescued 18 abducted members of the Frontier Corps, although 52 of their colleagues were still thought to be captives of suspected Taliban militants.

Since Sunday, the week’s offensive had killed more than 180 militants, while military forces had recorded one fatality and one wounded service member, Abbas said. He expressed hope that the campaign would conclude before the week ended.

Pakistan had requested helicopters, communications systems and night-vision equipment from the United States to support its forces, Abbas added Thursday.

The largest number of casualties that week occurred Tuesday, when Pakistani warplanes struck targets in Dir district, killing at least 70 militants, according to the military.

The fighting formed part of an expanded army campaign against the Taliban in Pakistan’s unstable tribal areas. Islamabad had faced criticism for failing to act forcefully enough against militants operating near the Afghan border.

The U.S. military had consequently launched strikes on militant sites inside Pakistan, creating friction between Washington and Islamabad. Pakistan’s own campaign did not appear to have brought an end to U.S. drone operations within the country.

Pakistani intelligence sources said a suspected pilotless aircraft killed six people Wednesday night in Kaniguran, a village in the South Waziristan tribal district close to Afghanistan.

Pakistan had repeatedly objected to what it described as U.S. air attacks on its territory. American military officials in Afghanistan had not addressed the strikes, which generally targeted Taliban combatants along the border. However, the United States was the only nation known to be operating in the area with the capacity to fire missiles from remotely controlled aircraft.

Speaking to reporters Wednesday night, U.S. President Barack Obama said he was “gravely concerned about the situation in Pakistan.”

At a news conference marking the end of his first 100 days as president, Obama said the United States had “huge national security interests in making sure that Pakistan is stable” and did not become a “nuclear-armed militant state.”

Nevertheless, he emphasized that his greater concern was whether Pakistan’s civilian authorities could “deliver basic services,” rather than the possibility “that they’re immediately going to be overrun” by Taliban forces.

The latest Pakistani offensive prompted large numbers of civilians to leave the area. Amnesty International reported that at least 33,000 people had fled their homes during the recent violence.

The U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees said those escaping Lower Dir in Pakistan’s North West Frontier Province were joining an existing displaced population of more than 500,000 people.

Abbas said the military had finished its effort to remove militants from Dir on Tuesday and had shifted its main attention to Buner. He said approximately 300 militants had moved into Buner several days earlier, violating a recent Taliban commitment to withdraw from the district.

Although Buner lies roughly 60 miles from Islamabad, Abbas maintained that the militants were not in a position to advance into the capital.

Pakistani fighter aircraft attacked locations in Buner and the Swat Valley to cut off routes used by militants to enter or leave the area, Abbas said.

CNN’s Samson Desta, Ivan Watson and Nasir Habib contributed to the report.

**Pakistani forces press Taliban offensive as civilians flee northwest**

**ISLAMABAD, Pakistan** — Pakistani troops backed by helicopter gunships and artillery intensified operations against Taliban militants in the northwestern districts of Lower Dir and Buner, military officials said, as fighting forced tens of thousands of civilians from their homes.

The military said scores of militants had been killed in the two districts, along with several soldiers. Officials at various stages of the offensive reported more than 70 militant deaths in Lower Dir and dozens more in Buner, although the figures could not be independently verified because access to the combat zones was restricted. Taliban representatives disputed some government casualty claims.

The operation began after militants moved from the Swat Valley into neighboring Buner, about 100 kilometers — 60 miles — from Islamabad. Their advance raised fears in Pakistan and abroad that a peace agreement in Swat had allowed the Taliban to expand its influence closer to the capital.

Elsewhere in Pakistan’s tribal region, suspected U.S. drones carried out missile strikes against compounds believed to be used by al Qaeda and Taliban fighters. Pakistani intelligence officials said the attacks killed several suspected militants, but reports also cited possible civilian casualties. Washington generally declined to comment on individual strikes, while Pakistan publicly protested that they violated its sovereignty and could increase anti-American sentiment.

U.S. President Barack Obama said he was “gravely concerned” about the stability of Pakistan’s civilian government, describing it as fragile while expressing confidence that the country’s nuclear arsenal remained secure. The Obama administration pressed Islamabad to treat the Taliban’s advance as an urgent threat.

The fighting created a growing humanitarian crisis. The United Nations and Pakistani relief agencies said tens of thousands of people had fled Dir and Buner, joining families already displaced by violence in Swat and the tribal areas. Many arrived in camps or crowded into relatives’ homes with limited food, water and medical care.

Aid officials warned that the number of displaced people could rise sharply if the military operation widened or prolonged fighting prevented residents from returning home.

**Pakistan Army Presses Offensive Against Taliban in Buner**  
*April 29, 2009*

**ISLAMABAD, Pakistan —** Pakistani troops backed by helicopter gunships pressed an offensive Wednesday against Taliban militants in the northwestern district of Buner, as the government sought to reverse an insurgent advance that had heightened concern in Washington about the stability of the nuclear-armed country.

Maj. Gen. Athar Abbas, the military’s chief spokesman, said security forces had entered key parts of Buner and were moving against militant positions. He said troops had been inserted by helicopter and had encountered resistance, with dozens of insurgents reported killed during the opening stages of the operation.

Abbas said the campaign was intended to clear Buner of militants who had moved into the district from neighboring Swat Valley. He described the operation as progressing satisfactorily but indicated that difficult fighting remained in the mountainous area.

The military’s push came after Taliban fighters spread into Buner despite a peace agreement under which the government accepted Islamic law in Swat and surrounding districts. The militants’ presence in Buner—about 60 miles, or 100 kilometers, from Islamabad—prompted warnings that the truce had allowed them to expand their influence rather than lay down their arms.

Pakistani officials said troops had secured government buildings and were advancing toward areas used by the militants. Communications with the district remained limited, and casualty figures could not be independently verified. Residents reported artillery fire and helicopter attacks, while civilians continued to flee villages near the fighting.

The offensive unfolded as President Barack Obama marked his 100th day in office. His administration has made Pakistan and neighboring Afghanistan central to its regional strategy and has repeatedly urged Islamabad to confront militant groups that threaten both Pakistani authority and U.S.-led forces across the Afghan border.

Pakistani leaders have rejected suggestions that the capital or the country’s nuclear arsenal faces an immediate threat. But the militants’ rapid movement into Buner intensified domestic and international pressure on the government to act.

Abbas said the army’s objective was to restore state control and allow displaced residents to return. The length of the operation, he said, would depend on the resistance offered by the militants and the difficulty of separating fighters from civilians in the rugged terrain.

counterfactuals.output:
### Pakistan intensifies campaign against Taliban in Dir and Buner

**ISLAMABAD —** Pakistan intensified military operations against Taliban militants in the northwestern districts of Lower Dir and Buner in spring 2009, after insurgents expanded beyond the Swat Valley and moved closer to the capital.

In **Lower Dir**, troops backed by artillery and helicopter gunships attacked militant positions, particularly around the Maidan area. The army said the offensive targeted fighters who had violated a peace agreement and attacked security forces. Heavy clashes, roadblocks and curfews restricted movement, while communications with some villages were disrupted.

Security forces also launched an operation in **Buner**, roughly 100 kilometers from Islamabad, after Taliban fighters entered the district, occupied government buildings and established checkpoints. Troops sought to regain control of key roads and the district headquarters at Daggar. Officials reported substantial militant casualties, although independent confirmation was difficult because journalists and aid workers had limited access.

The Taliban advance heightened concern in Islamabad and Washington about the government’s ability to prevent insurgents from extending their control. Pakistani officials asked the United States to expedite military assistance, including **helicopters and spare parts, night-vision equipment, communications systems, and other counterinsurgency and surveillance gear**. Washington indicated it was prepared to accelerate support, while stressing that the campaign had to be led by Pakistan.

The fighting imposed a severe burden on civilians. **Tens of thousands initially fled Dir and Buner**, joining families already displaced from Swat and neighboring tribal areas; the number rose sharply as the wider offensive continued. Many residents left on foot or in crowded vehicles, often with little warning. Others remained trapped by curfews, blocked roads and continuing shelling.

Displaced families crowded into relatives’ homes, schools and temporary camps, where shortages of food, clean water, medical care and sanitation were reported. Aid agencies warned that prolonged fighting could produce a much larger humanitarian emergency and urged the government to establish safe evacuation routes and allow relief workers reliable access.

Pakistani authorities described the operations as necessary to reverse the Taliban’s territorial gains. Local residents, however, faced danger from both militant coercion and the army’s use of heavy weapons in populated areas, underscoring the civilian cost of the campaign.

counterfactuals.output:
**Pakistan’s 2009 Taliban War Deepens Fears for Nuclear-Armed State’s Stability**

**ISLAMABAD, Pakistan — December 2009** — Pakistan’s battle against Taliban militants escalated into one of the country’s most serious internal conflicts in 2009, leaving thousands of combatants and civilians dead, forcing millions from their homes and intensifying international concern over the stability of the nuclear-armed state.

During two major offensives—first in the northwestern Swat Valley and later in the tribal region of South Waziristan—the Pakistani military said it killed more than 2,000 suspected militants. Several hundred soldiers and paramilitary troops were also reported killed during the year, although precise totals remained difficult to verify because journalists and independent observers had limited access to combat areas.

The fighting was accompanied by suicide bombings, assassinations and attacks on security installations across Pakistan. Taliban militants struck police academies, army facilities, markets and mosques, bringing the conflict far beyond the remote mountain districts where the insurgency had taken root.

### Military moves into Swat

The first major campaign began in the spring, after militants associated with cleric Maulana Fazlullah expanded from the Swat Valley into neighboring Buner district, less than 100 kilometers from Islamabad. Their advance alarmed Pakistani officials and foreign governments, which feared that a peace agreement allowing Islamic law in parts of the northwest had strengthened rather than contained the insurgents.

In late April and early May, the army launched an offensive later known as **Operation Rah-e-Rast**, or “Path of Righteousness.” Helicopter gunships, artillery and ground troops attacked Taliban positions in Mingora, Swat’s largest city, and in surrounding valleys.

Pakistani commanders said the operation broke the militants’ control of the region and killed large numbers of fighters. The army reported roughly 2,000 militant deaths during the Swat campaign and acknowledged hundreds of military casualties across the broader fighting. The government’s figures could not be independently confirmed, and rights organizations warned that civilians had also been killed by shelling, airstrikes, roadside bombs and militant reprisals.

At the height of the operation, more than two million people fled Swat, Buner and nearby districts. Many crowded into camps or stayed with relatives in other parts of the North-West Frontier Province, now known as Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. The displacement became one of the world’s largest humanitarian emergencies that year.

### Hostages and captured Frontier Corps troops

Militants also abducted members of the **Frontier Corps**, the paramilitary force deployed throughout the tribal belt and northwest. In several incidents, Taliban fighters overran or ambushed isolated checkpoints, seizing personnel and carrying them into militant-controlled territory.

Some kidnapped Frontier Corps members were later released through negotiations conducted by tribal elders, while others were reported killed or remained missing. The captures exposed weaknesses in local security units, which often operated from poorly defended posts and faced militants familiar with the terrain.

The abductions carried particular symbolic weight. The Frontier Corps was intended to serve as the state’s front line in the border regions, but its personnel were frequently drawn from the same Pashtun communities in which the Taliban recruited. Militants used captured troops for bargaining, propaganda and pressure on the government to halt military operations or free prisoners.

### War shifts to South Waziristan

After retaking the main population centers in Swat, Pakistan turned its attention to South Waziristan, the stronghold of the Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan, or TTP. The organization had been led by Baitullah Mehsud, who was accused by Pakistani and American officials of orchestrating suicide bombings and the 2007 assassination of former Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto. The TTP denied involvement in Bhutto’s death.

Mehsud was reported killed in August in a missile strike believed to have been carried out by a United States drone. Neither Washington nor Islamabad publicly acknowledged many such operations at the time, but Pakistani intelligence officials regularly attributed the explosions to remotely piloted American aircraft operating from across the border in Afghanistan or from secret regional bases.

Hakimullah Mehsud subsequently emerged as the TTP’s leader.

In October, about 30,000 Pakistani troops launched **Operation Rah-e-Nijat**, or “Path of Salvation,” against militant positions in South Waziristan. The army said hundreds of insurgents were killed as troops entered towns and valleys controlled by the Mehsud faction. Military casualties mounted as militants used mines, improvised explosive devices, ambushes and suicide attacks.

The army captured several important bases and declared that the militants’ territorial control had been broken. Many TTP commanders and fighters, however, appeared to have escaped into neighboring tribal districts, Afghanistan or remote mountain areas, raising doubts about whether the offensive had destroyed the organization or merely dispersed it.

### Suspected American drone strikes

The conflict unfolded alongside an expanding campaign of suspected American drone attacks in Pakistan’s federally administered tribal areas. Missiles struck compounds, vehicles and militant gathering places in North and South Waziristan, killing senior Al Qaeda and Taliban figures as well as lower-level fighters.

U.S. officials argued privately that the strikes removed militants involved in attacks on NATO forces in Afghanistan and plots abroad. Pakistani officials publicly protested that the attacks violated national sovereignty and fueled anti-American anger, even as reports suggested some elements of the government quietly cooperated with the program.

Casualty figures from the drone strikes were sharply disputed. Local officials and intelligence sources often described those killed as militants, while residents and human-rights organizations said civilians were among the dead. Restrictions on access made independent verification exceptionally difficult.

The reported killing of Baitullah Mehsud was cited by supporters as evidence of the drones’ effectiveness. Critics countered that each strike risked driving more recruits toward the Taliban and undermining the Pakistani government’s legitimacy.

### Taliban retaliation spreads nationwide

As the army advanced, the Taliban widened its campaign of retaliation. Bombings struck Peshawar, Lahore, Rawalpindi and Islamabad. In October, militants attacked the army’s General Headquarters in Rawalpindi, taking hostages during a siege near the center of Pakistan’s military establishment.

Other attacks targeted intelligence offices, police stations and crowded markets. A bombing in a Peshawar market in October killed more than 100 people, many of them women and children. In December, gunmen and suicide bombers attacked a mosque in Rawalpindi frequented by military officers and their families, killing dozens.

The attacks demonstrated that militants remained capable of operating in Pakistan’s major cities despite battlefield losses in the northwest.

### International fears over Pakistan’s future

The violence heightened longstanding fears about Pakistan’s political and economic stability. Foreign governments were particularly concerned about the security of the country’s nuclear arsenal, although Pakistani and American officials repeatedly said the weapons were protected by multiple layers of security and were not in danger of falling into militant hands.

The greater immediate threat, analysts said, was the possibility of prolonged insurgency eroding public confidence, weakening government institutions and aggravating divisions within the military and intelligence services.

Pakistan was also under intense pressure from Washington to prevent Afghan Taliban and allied networks from using its territory to attack U.S. and NATO troops across the border. Pakistani leaders insisted that their armed forces were already fighting an existential war and accused foreign critics of underestimating the human and economic cost.

By the end of 2009, the government had re-established formal control over much of Swat and key areas of South Waziristan. But the Taliban’s ability to retreat, reorganize and carry out mass-casualty attacks showed that the conflict was far from over.

The year left Pakistan with devastated communities, hundreds of thousands of people still displaced, a strained military and an insurgency transformed from a remote frontier rebellion into a nationwide security threat.
